What Do Foreign Trends Tell Us About Future U.S. Labor Force Dynamics?

Jeffrey B. Dawson, Matthew Higgins, and Chanwoo Kim

Growth in the U.S. working-age population has fallen to near zero with the recent sharp drop in net immigration. Given the ongoing decline in the native-born working-age population, the available labor supply could soon begin to shrink. The demographic path the U.S. may soon navigate has already been trod by several other advanced economies that have experienced more rapid population aging and historically lower immigration. This post lays out the basic facts about advanced economy (AE) experiences since 2014 and raises the prospect that the demographic headwinds long visible abroad may now be coming into clear view at home.

Demographic and Labor Force Trends

The table below shows percentage changes in three variables from 2014 to 2025: working-age (ages 15-64) populations, prime-age (ages 25-54) populations, and the active population, or labor force. The countries shown are the sixteen largest AEs, ordered by economic size. We also show median values for a larger set of thirty-six AEs and for developments in China, at the bottom of the table.

The first column shows wide variation in the growth of working-age populations. Growth has been negative for seven of the countries shown, with particularly marked declines in Japan, Italy, Poland, and Taiwan. Growth has also been negative in the median AE. Yet several countries have seen gains of more than 5 percent. Growth in the U.S. was solidly positive at 3 percent, but not near the top.

Variation in the growth of prime-age populations, shown in the second column, has been still more striking, ranging from dramatic declines (Japan, Germany, Italy, and Spain) to marked increases (Canada, Australia, and Sweden). Again, the U.S. stands toward the higher end of the distribution. Larger declines in the prime-age population than in the working-age population (note the gap in Spain) imply that a large share of the population has moved into the 55-64 age group and will drop out of the traditional working-age population over the coming decade. As we’ll see shortly, the variation in countries’ demographic trajectories is mostly an immigration story.

The third column of the table shows labor force growth since 2014. The contrast with demographic developments is stark. Where working-age populations have grown, active populations have grown more strongly; where working-age populations have declined, active populations have defied demographic gravity. (Indeed, in our broader sample of thirty-six AEs, only Greece and Latvia saw small labor force declines.) In several cases, the contrast can only be termed remarkable. Japan, for example, saw 6 percent labor force growth on a 7 percent drop in its working-age population. Germany saw almost 6 percent growth on a 2 percent decline in its working-age population—and a drop of more than 8 percent in the high-attachment prime-age population.

A Boost from Labor Force Participation

The gap between growth in active and working-age populations implies that labor force participation has been increasing. The table below illustrates this phenomenon across three dimensions, showing changes in participation rates among the traditional working-age population (ages 15-64), working-age women, and the “young old” (ages 65 to 74).

As shown in the first column, the trend toward increased participation has been essentially universal across AEs. Gains in several countries peaked at 5 percentage points (ppt), with the median country seeing an increase of 4 ppt. Higher participation among women made an important contribution to the general increase, with the median country seeing an increase of more than 5 ppt. Participation among the “young old” was also up strongly, with Japan leading the way at roughly 12½ ppt, and Korea and the Netherlands not too far behind. The median gain clocked in at above 5½ ppt. Note that participation gains in the U.S., while positive, have been below AE norms across all three dimensions of the participation data.

How Much Participation Upside?

Increased labor force participation has kept AE labor forces growing even where working-age populations have been shrinking. But participation rates can’t keep rising forever: Demography is eventually destiny.

As shown in the first column, the median AE participation rate for the 15-64 population stood just below 79 percent in 2025. Participation was highest in Japan and several countries in north or central Europe, and lowest in Italy. A generally similar geographical pattern holds for female participation (second column). Participation among the 65-74 population is strikingly heterogeneous (third column). Korea and Japan show very high participation among this age group, while participation in the U.S. is moderately high. In contrast, many European countries show much lower rates, notably France and Spain.

Mechanically, low current participation suggests an upside to the labor force. For concreteness, we consider the implications of increasing working-age participation rates to 85 percent, roughly the current frontier. In Italy, the impact would be the same as a 26 percent increase in the working-age population, given current participation rates. For the U.S., the corresponding increase in the engaged working-age population would be roughly 13 percent. Of course, the fact that this upside exists provides no reason to believe that it will be tapped.

The potential increase in the engaged “young old” population is greater, given lower current participation rates. We have no way of judging, however, whether the very high rates currently seen in Japan or Korea are realistically achievable elsewhere. Still, increases in “young old” participation can have an outsized impact on aggregate labor force growth, given the growing relative size of this age group.

Korea already sits at the AE frontier for “young old” participation, alongside Japan, which means there is comparatively little remaining upside from this margin. With participation projected by the Bank of Korea to peak around 2028 and then decline, the participation buffer is likely to shift from an offset to a drag. And because net immigration, discussed below, remains limited and is not expected to rise materially, Korea offers a preview of how quickly labor force growth can slow once participation gains are exhausted.

The Contribution of Immigration 

Given the widespread focus on population aging in advanced economies, it’s notable that a number of AEs have seen strong recent growth in their working-age populations. Immigration, not fecundity, is the explanation. Every advanced economy (outside Israel) saw fertility fall below replacement levels by the early- to mid-1970s, something that would have weighed on working-age population declines dating back to the 1990s.

We don’t have good data on current migrant stocks by age group for most AEs. Yet the available evidence on the contribution of immigration to growth in working-age populations is compelling. As shown in chart below, every country that saw working-age populations rise from 2014 to 2025 recorded substantial net immigration, equivalent to at least several percentage points of the initial working‑age population stock. Notably, relative to its size, the U.S. does not particularly stand out as a destination. Immigration did more to boost working-age populations in the UK, Sweden, and Switzerland, and several other countries. Whether AE labor force growth can continue will of course depend critically on the scale of future immigration flows.

The Road Ahead

Across advanced economies, immigration has been the key factor sustaining growth in working-age populations, while rising participation has temporarily offset demographic pressures even where populations are shrinking. But participation gains are finite, and countries with limited immigration have already seen how quickly labor force growth can slow once this margin is exhausted. For the U.S.—now facing similar demographic headwinds—the experience of other AEs underscores that future labor supply will depend increasingly on policy choices around immigration and participation.
